title: Kautilya's Arthashastra

cards.b:
The Arthashastra is a detailed manual on how to run a state: its economy, army, spies, laws and foreign policy. Tradition credits it to Kautilya, also called Chanakya or Vishnugupta, the minister of Chandragupta Maurya (c. 4th century BCE).

The text was lost for centuries. R. Shamasastry found a manuscript and published it in 1909, with an English translation in 1915.

Scholars such as Thomas Trautmann and Patrick Olivelle think the text we have was compiled and revised over time, reaching its final form around the early centuries CE.

cards.h: Artha: the science of wealth and power
cards.b:
Artha means material well-being. Kautilya says artha is the most important of the three goals of life (dharma, artha and kama), because the other two depend on it.

The state's job is to gain and protect territory and to bring yogakshema, the welfare and security of its people.

"In the happiness of his subjects lies the happiness of the king."
Arthashastra 1.19

So Kautilya's realism serves welfare, not just the ruler's ego.

A state has seven limbs, in order of importance: swami (king), amatya (ministers), janapada (territory and people), durga (fortified city), kosha (treasury), danda (army) and mitra (ally). It is an organic view: if one limb fails, the whole body suffers.

The diagram shows one line of the circle. The mandala theory places the would-be conqueror (vijigishu) at the centre of a circle of states. The immediate neighbour is a natural enemy, and the state beyond is a natural friend. Two more states matter: the madhyama (middle king) and the udasina (a neutral king stronger than both).

Kautilya lists six measures of foreign policy:

  • Sandhi: peace or treaty.
  • Vigraha: hostility or war.
  • Asana: staying quiet, watching.
  • Yana: marching, preparing to attack.
  • Samshraya: seeking shelter with a stronger power.
  • Dvaidhibhava: the double policy: peace with one, war with another.

The choice depends on whether you are weaker, equal or stronger. He also lists four means: sama (persuasion), dana (gifts), bheda (division) and danda (force).

• A large salaried bureaucracy with superintendents (adhyakshas) for mines, trade, forests and more.
  • A strong treasury: "all undertakings depend on the treasury."
  • A detailed network of spies (gudhapurushas) to test ministers and watch the public.
  • Testing ministers (upadha) through temptations of dharma, wealth, desire and fear.
  • The king's day is divided into sixteen parts, each with set duties.

Max Weber said that compared with this book, Machiavelli's Prince is harmless.

Kautilya names four sources of law: dharma (sacred law), vyavahara (evidence and transactions), charitra (custom) and rajashasana (the king's edict).

Strikingly, he says that when they conflict, the king's edict, if based on justice, prevails. This raises the state's authority above tradition.

Punishment should be neither too harsh nor too mild. Too harsh, and people fear the king. Too mild, and people despise him. Just punishment brings dharma, artha and kama.

• Both are realists. Both put the state's survival first and accept deceit and force.
  • Kautilya is far more comprehensive: economy, law, welfare and war. Machiavelli wrote a short book of advice.
  • Kautilya ties the king to dharma and welfare. Machiavelli separates politics from Christian ethics.
  • Kautilya wanted stability and expansion; Machiavelli wanted Italian unity in a crisis.

Some scholars call Kautilya India's first theorist of a welfare state.

cards.h: Economy and welfare in the Arthashastra
cards.b:
The Arthashastra imagines an active, almost interventionist state.

  • The state runs mines, forests, weaving, liquor and salt, and sets up state farms (sita land).
  • Superintendents fix weights and measures, control prices and check traders' profits.
  • The king must support orphans, the old, the sick and helpless women.
  • Labour contracts and wages are regulated. Masters who mistreat workers are fined.
  • Settling new land (janapada nivesha) and building irrigation are royal duties.

This is why some scholars call Kautilya's state a kind of early welfare state. Others warn that its aim was revenue and power, with welfare as a means to keep people productive and loyal.

India's diplomatic enclave in New Delhi is called Chanakyapuri.

Strategic thinkers use the mandala idea to read India's neighbourhood: hostile neighbours (Pakistan, at times China) and the value of friends beyond them, such as Afghanistan, Iran, the Central Asian states and the Indo-Pacific partners.

Shivshankar Menon, a former National Security Adviser, and analysts at the Institute for Defence Studies and Analyses (IDSA) have written on Kautilya's relevance to Indian strategy.

quiz.q: Who rediscovered and published the Arthashastra in 1909?
quiz.w: R. Shamasastry published it in 1909, with a translation in 1915.

quiz.q: In mandala theory, the immediate neighbour is a natural…
quiz.w: The neighbour is the natural enemy; the neighbour's neighbour is a friend.

o: Peace with one, war with another

quiz.q: When sources of law conflict, Kautilya says the deciding source is…
quiz.w: Rajashasana, the king's edict based on justice, prevails.

o: Welfare and security of the people
quiz.w: The state's goal is the welfare and security of its subjects.

quiz.q: The four means (upayas) are sama, dana, bheda and…
Testing ministers through temptations is called…
quiz.w: Upadha: tests of dharma, wealth, desire and fear.

o: A neutral king stronger than the others
quiz.w: A powerful neutral state outside the rivalry.
